fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a question I find really interesting, because if you think about it, these models are all trained on roughly the same internet. The pretraining corpora overlap enormously. Everybody has Common Crawl, everybody has GitHub, everybody has the same books and papers. And the architectures have mostly converged too. It's a decoder-only transformer with some flavor of attention and some flavor of mixture of experts. So on paper you'd expect the outputs to look pretty similar. And yet, if you show me a few paragraphs from each of the major providers, I can usually guess which one it came from. There's a recognizable voice.

My view is that most of what you're recognizing comes from post-training, not pretraining. Pretraining gives you a kind of shared substrate. There's this idea floating around that representations converge as models scale, and I think that's roughly right at the base model level. The base models are more alike than they are different. But then each lab does its own supervised fine-tuning and its own preference optimization, and that's where the personality gets stamped on. The data for that stage is tiny compared to pretraining, but it's extremely high leverage. If your annotators are told to prefer bullet points and a cheerful summary at the end, you get a model that does that everywhere. If your reward model slightly rewards hedging, you get a model that hedges. Those small biases compound because the model sees them consistently across every example.

And it's not only the annotators. It's the written guidelines, the constitution or spec or whatever each lab calls it, the system prompt that gets baked in, the choice of which refusals to train in. Those are human decisions by a fairly small group of people at each company, and they're quite path dependent. Someone decided early on that the model should sound a certain way, that became the training signal, and it's hard to undo later.

There's also a more technical piece that I think gets underrated, which is the sampling and decoding setup. Temperature, repetition penalties, how long the model is encouraged to go before it stops. Those are product choices, and they shape the texture of the text more than people realize.

I'll say one thing from my own background, which is more on the architecture and data side. I used to believe architecture mattered a lot for these kinds of qualitative differences, and I've mostly changed my mind. When we did the ConvNeXt work, the lesson was that a lot of the supposed gaps between model families came down to training recipes, not the architecture itself. I think the same thing is happening with language models. The data pipeline and the post-training recipe explain almost all the recognizable differences, and the architecture explains almost none of it.

So the short answer is: same substrate, different last mile. And the last mile is where the humans are.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says annotator preferences and guidelines systematically shape model behavior, giving examples such as bullet points, cheerful summaries, and hedging.

r002.rationale: It attributes recognizable output differences to provider choices, but does not clearly identify outputs as a proxy for otherwise unknown development differences.

r003.rationale: It directly states that post-training accounts for most recognizable differences and includes provider-designed system prompts among the influential choices.

opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is something we looked at fairly directly. The starting observation was simple: if you take responses from ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek and so on, and train a classifier to predict which model wrote a given response, it works surprisingly well. It's not slightly above chance. It's very high accuracy, well above ninety percent in the five-way setting. So these models have quite distinct fingerprints, even though at a high level they're all "helpful assistants" trained on roughly the same internet.

Then the interesting question is where those fingerprints come from. We tried to take the text apart in different ways.

The first factor is word choice. If you shuffle the words in a response, so all the syntax and meaning are mostly destroyed and you basically have a bag of words, the classifier still does very well. Each model has favorite words and phrases. Some lean on "certainly" or "delve" or "it's important to note." Others prefer "based on" or "according to." These are small lexical habits, but they're very consistent.

The second factor is formatting. Things like how heavily a model uses markdown, headers, bold text, bullet lists versus paragraphs, how it structures a conclusion. Strip the text down to just the formatting skeleton, and you can still tell a lot.

The third factor, which surprised me a bit, is semantics. If you have another model rewrite or paraphrase a response, so the surface wording changes, you can still identify the original source quite well. That suggests the differences aren't only stylistic. They're also in what the model chooses to say, what it emphasizes, how it frames an answer. Summarization reduces the signal more, because it removes detail, but it doesn't eliminate it.

On why this happens, I think the main driver is post-training. Pretraining corpora overlap a lot between labs. Supervised fine-tuning data, preference data, the people who write and rate those responses, the reward models, and the system prompts are much more specific to each company. Each lab has its own idea of what a good response looks like, and RLHF or similar methods push the model hard toward that target. So the model converges to a house style. Small preferences in the reward signal get amplified into very consistent habits. Supporting this, models from the same family, say different sizes from one provider, are much harder to tell apart than models from different providers.

I find this connected to earlier work I did on dataset bias in vision. There, we showed a neural network can tell which large image dataset a picture came from, even though those datasets were built to be diverse and general. Same lesson here: whenever data goes through a particular pipeline with particular choices, it picks up a signature, and neural networks are very good at picking up signatures.

There's also a practical consequence. A lot of people now train models on synthetic data generated by other models. If you distill from one provider's outputs, you inherit its idiosyncrasies, and you can detect that afterward. So these fingerprints are useful for questions like "which model was this trained on?" and for thinking about how similar our models are really becoming.

r001.rationale: The response mentions provider-specific preference data and people who write and rate responses, but it does not explain how differing instructions to post-training annotators systematically shape behavior.

r002.rationale: It presents model outputs as distinctive fingerprints that can reveal the originating provider and expose inherited training choices, thereby serving as an indirect proxy for development differences.

r003.rationale: It explicitly identifies post-training as the main driver and includes provider-specific system prompts among the choices that create recognizable output differences.

fable-5.text:
That's a question we actually got curious enough about to study systematically. We trained simple classifiers to look at a response and predict which model produced it, and the striking thing is how easy that turns out to be — you can get well above ninety percent accuracy distinguishing outputs from, say, ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and open models like Llama. So these differences aren't subtle vibes people imagine; they're real, measurable signatures.

Where do they come from? There are a few layers. The most obvious one is formatting and lexical habits. Each provider's post-training instills very characteristic patterns — how much markdown they use, whether they love bullet points and headers, certain phrases they reach for constantly. Some models say "certainly" or "delve" far more than others. If you strip out the exact words by replacing them with their part-of-speech tags, or remove the formatting, classification accuracy drops, so a lot of the signal lives there.

But the more interesting finding is that it doesn't all live there. If you take an output and have another model paraphrase or even summarize it — so the surface wording is completely rewritten — a classifier can still tell which model originally produced it at rates way above chance. That tells you the differences go deeper than style. They're partly semantic: models differ in what they choose to talk about, how they structure an explanation, how much they hedge, what level of detail they default to. That's shaped by the post-training data — the human preference data, the instruction-tuning examples, the reward models — which each lab curates differently and which encodes a particular taste about what a good answer looks like.

And there's one more factor I find fascinating, which is that these idiosyncrasies propagate. A lot of open models are trained partly on synthetic data distilled from stronger proprietary models, and you can see the fingerprints transfer — a model trained on another model's outputs starts to inherit its signature. So in a sense you can read the training lineage off the outputs. It raises real questions for the ecosystem, because if everyone trains on everyone else's generations, you might expect convergence and a loss of diversity in these model "personalities" over time. For now, though, each provider's choices in data and post-training leave a surprisingly legible stamp on everything their models say.

opus-5.text:
It's a great question, because for a long time this was folklore — people would say "oh, that sounds like a ChatGPT answer" — and we wanted to know whether there was actually signal there or whether it was just vibes.

So we ran the obvious experiment: take outputs from several models on the same prompts, train a simple text classifier to predict which model produced each one. It gets it right the overwhelming majority of the time. Not 60%, not 70% — it's in the high nineties. These models are far more distinguishable than people assume.

Then the interesting part is asking what the classifier is keying on. A lot of it is surface-level: markdown habits, how aggressively a model reaches for bulleted lists versus prose, whether it bolds header phrases, particular transition words, how it opens and closes a response. Each provider has its own house style. But the striking thing is what happens when you take that away — strip the formatting, paraphrase everything into uniform prose, even reduce the text to just its parts of speech. Accuracy drops, but it stays well above chance. So there's something deeper than typography. There are differences in which semantic territory a model wanders into, how it decomposes a problem, what it thinks is worth caveating.

Where does it come from? Mostly post-training, I'd argue. The pretraining corpora overlap enormously — everyone is reading the same internet. What differs is the preference data, the annotation guidelines, the reward models, the taste of the people shaping the final behavior. And there's a transmission effect: when you fine-tune on another model's outputs, you inherit its fingerprint. We could detect that. Which is a somewhat uncomfortable property, if you think about what it implies for provenance.

r001.rationale: The response attributes provider differences to distinct preference data, annotation guidelines, reward models, and shaping tastes, explaining how post-training practices produce different behaviors.

r002.rationale: It uses model outputs and a classifier to detect provider-specific fingerprints, then connects those detectable differences to otherwise hidden model-development choices.

r003.rationale: The response says differences come mostly from post-training but never identifies provider-designed system prompts as a major cause.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think it comes mostly from the data and the post-training recipe, and a lot less from the architecture. The pretraining corpora across providers overlap heavily, since everyone is scraping roughly the same internet. What differs is what happens afterward: the instruction-tuning data, the preference data, the reward models, the style guidelines the annotators follow, and increasingly the synthetic data generated by other models. Each of those nudges the model toward certain ways of phrasing things, and those nudges compound.

This is something we looked at directly. We trained a simple classifier to tell which model wrote a given response, and it was surprisingly accurate, much higher than I expected. Even when you ask a human to look at the outputs, you get a vague feeling that "this sounds like model X," but a classifier can pick up on it reliably. When we dug into what it was using, a lot of it was at the word level: particular openings, particular transition phrases, particular choices of vocabulary and formatting. Some models love markdown and bullet structure, and some are more conversational. Some begin with an affirmation, and some jump straight into the content.

What surprised me more was that the signal didn't disappear when we rewrote or paraphrased the outputs. If you have another model rewrite the text and strip out surface cues, the classifier still does quite well, so the differences also live in the semantic content, meaning what the model chooses to say and how it organizes an answer, not only in the surface phrasing.

There's also a feedback loop. If you fine-tune a model on another model's outputs, it tends to inherit those idiosyncrasies, so as more training data becomes model-generated, I'd expect the fingerprints to propagate and in some cases get amplified. I can't say precisely which stage contributes the most, and I suspect it's a mix of the data mixture, the alignment process, and the synthetic data. But my intuition is that post-training is where most of the separation happens, because that's where each provider deliberately shapes the personality and style of the model.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it comes from choices made after pretraining. Most labs start from a broadly similar mix of web text, code, and books, so the pretraining mix matters, but I'd guess the bigger differences come from what each team decides a good answer looks like. How long should it be? How much should it hedge? When should it refuse? Should it lead with the direct answer or with caveats? Those preferences get baked in through human and AI feedback, and each organization's rubric is different.

What a team is optimizing for also shows up everywhere. If a lot of effort goes into coding or long agentic tasks, that orientation leaks into casual conversation too. The voice people recognize is really an accumulation of many small decisions by many people, not one setting someone turned.

I'd also be careful about overreading the differences. Much of the similarity across providers is convergent, since they train on overlapping data with similar recipes. So the distinct styles are partly real design choices and partly just which part of a shared distribution each lab chose to emphasize.

r002.rationale: It links recognizable output styles to development decisions, but does not clearly identify outputs as a proxy for otherwise unknown provider differences.

r003.rationale: It attributes major differences to post-pretraining choices and feedback, but does not mention provider-designed system prompts or clearly make the full stated judgment.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of it comes from post-training. There isn’t one uniquely correct way to answer most questions. You can give a short answer, explain everything in detail, ask a follow-up question—all of those might be reasonable. But when you train the model to prefer certain responses, you’re making choices about what a good assistant should sound like. Different teams make different choices, and those choices become recognizable.

The pretraining data probably matters too, as do the instructions around the model when you use it. So I wouldn’t attribute everything to one stage. But my intuition is that the personality you notice—the tone, how verbose it is, how confidently it responds—is especially sensitive to post-training. In some sense, you’re seeing the preferences of the people who shaped the model.

sol-6.1.text:
My guess is that a lot of it comes from post-training. You’re making choices about what a good response should look like: should it be concise, should it explain every step, how cautious should it be? Those choices get reflected in the examples and preference feedback you train on, and eventually they become a recognizable style.

The pretraining data and training recipe can also contribute, of course. But the answer we see is already shaped by several stages of training. So I’d be careful about interpreting a difference in how two models speak as necessarily a difference in their underlying capabilities. Some of it may simply be that they’ve been trained to express those capabilities differently.

sol-5.6.text: I think a lot of it comes down to the post-training recipe. The base models may be trained on broadly similar data with similar objectives, but providers make different choices about instruction tuning, preference data, safety policies, system prompts, and even decoding. Those choices encode a kind of house style—how concise the model is, how cautious it is, how directly it answers, and whether it tends to hedge or elaborate. So the differences people recognize are not necessarily just differences in raw capability; they’re also differences in what each provider has optimized the model to sound like and prioritize.

luna-5.6.text:
I think it’s a combination of the entire pipeline, not just the underlying model architecture. Different providers train on different mixtures of data, apply different filtering and deduplication, and make different choices about the training objective. Then the post-training stage—human feedback, preference data, safety tuning, and instruction tuning—has a huge effect on how a model phrases things, how cautious it is, and what it considers a useful answer.

There are also differences at inference time: system prompts, decoding settings, tool use, and even how the model is asked to handle uncertainty. So what people recognize as a provider’s “style” is really the fingerprint of all those decisions taken together. It’s less like one isolated design choice and more like the result of a whole stack of data, optimization, and product choices.
